job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I reviewed only the text you pasted, not the pre-amendment version or the underlying statutes. Items are grouped by theme, and the numbering runs straight through.

## Definitions and scope

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton test applies to "a single vessel," so an operator can run several vessels, each under the line, or rotate vessels and recover far more in aggregate. There is no aggregation or affiliated-entity rule.

2. **§2(1)(A), measurement.** "Per year" is undefined (calendar, rolling, license year?), as are "recovery" and whether tons are wet or dry, measured at the seabed, at the surface, or after processing. Nodules carry significant water weight, so the method can decide whether a vessel crosses the threshold.

3. **§2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" and the 200 m depth.** This may reach beyond deep-ocean mining, such as offshore sand and gravel or shelf-depth dredging, which makes the bill overbroad and mismatched with its "deep seabed" title. "Seabed" is also undefined, so it is unclear whether the bill covers deposits beneath the seabed or material taken from sediment plumes.

4. **§2(1)(B), Secretary's determination.** "The Secretary" is never identified (Commerce? Interior? State, the only Secretary named elsewhere, in §6?). The provision sets no process, notice, deadline, or standard beyond "comparable" risk. Paired with the criminal penalties in §5(b), it invites vagueness, nondelegation, and fair-notice challenges, and it is unclear whether a determination applies only prospectively.

5. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition covers only citizens and corporations organized under a State's laws. It omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, nonprofits, permanent residents, DC- or territory-organized entities, and foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies. With no ownership or control test, a foreign subsidiary can do what its U.S. parent cannot.

6. **§2(3), "covered vessel."** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold has no relationship to the mining threshold in §2(1), so smaller vessels, barges, platforms, or fleets of small vessels can mine without registering. "Equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources" is also unclear for leased or temporary equipment.

7. **Undefined terms generally.** "Person," "operator," "exploration license," "environmental assessment," "recovery," and "vessel" are all undefined. Each is a potential litigation hook, especially "operator" (owner, charterer, or contractor?).

## The prohibition (§3)

8. **§3(a), jurisdictional reach.** The bill covers "any person in the United States" and U.S. persons anywhere. It is unclear whether "in the United States" includes the EEZ, the continental shelf, or U.S.-flag vessels at sea. Foreign companies on foreign-flag vessels are outside the bill entirely, and reflagging or using foreign affiliates avoids it.

9. **§3(a), conduct covered.** Only "engag[ing] in" mining is banned. Financing, chartering, equipment supply, processing, and importing or selling seabed-mined minerals are not addressed, so U.S. firms could buy or process material mined by others.

10. **§3(b), grandfathering scope.** "Exploration license" has no stated issuer, so it could include licenses from foreign states or international bodies. It is also unclear whether the clause protects commercial recovery or only exploration. There is no cap on volume, area, or duration, and no treatment of renewals, amendments, transfers, or pending applications.

11. **§3(b), timing and conditions.** The cutoff is the date of enactment, but the ban doesn't take effect for another 180 days, which creates an incentive to rush licenses through. "Mining conducted under" a license doesn't say whether activity outside the license terms loses protection, and there is no revocation mechanism.

12. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** There is no definition, permit, approval, volume cap, duration limit, or bar on selling recovered material. Because it turns on "purpose," which is hard to prove, it could serve as a route to large-scale test mining.

13. **Relationship to existing law.** The bill neither amends nor addresses the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. ch. 26, as I recall it), under which NOAA issues exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits, or the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. Holders of commercial recovery permits (not mentioned in §3(b)) may argue the older, more specific licensing scheme controls. Please verify these cross-references against current code.

## Registry (§4)

14. **§4, no consequence for noncompliance.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false report carries no stated penalty. The registry is effectively unenforceable except through general false-statement law, which the bill doesn't invoke.

15. **§4(a), registration mechanics.** There is no deadline, no required content, no application to foreign-flag vessels, and no grant of rulemaking authority or fee/appropriations mechanism for NOAA. The bill also never says what registration is for, such as verifying grandfathered status.

16. **§4(b), reports.** The bill specifies no required content (location, tonnage, destination of material), verification standard, audit or inspection authority, vessel tracking, or public availability. Quarterly reports against an annual threshold also mean violations may surface only after the fact.

## Penalties and enforcement (§5)

17. **§5(a), no enforcement machinery.** The bill doesn't say who assesses the civil penalty or by what process, and it sets no factors, inflation adjustment, or collection mechanism. It also grants no investigation, inspection, boarding, seizure, forfeiture, or injunctive authority, and gives no role to the Coast Guard or citizen suits.

18. **§5(a) vs. §8, retroactivity conflict.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. That could be read to reach conduct during the gap, inviting due process and fair-notice challenges, or be disregarded as inconsistent with §8.

19. **§5(a), "each day."** A per-day penalty fits poorly with an offense defined by annual tonnage. It is unclear when a violation begins or how daily counts accrue, and no statute of limitations is specified.

20. **§5(b), "willfully."** It is undefined, and with thresholds and discretionary determinations the government may have to prove the defendant knew the activity was covered. That gives defendants a good-faith-misunderstanding defense. There is also no forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or proceeds.

21. **§5, who is liable.** There is no express liability for corporate parents, officers, or vessels in rem. Shell-company and subsidiary structures could shield the real beneficiaries.

## International and duration provisions (§§6–8)

22. **§6, negotiation mandate.** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" doesn't say whether the deadline is for starting or concluding talks, and "seek" is hortatory. "Equivalent" prohibitions is undefined, the form of agreement (treaty or executive) is unspecified, and there is no reporting requirement or consequence for missing the deadline.

23. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal contradiction.** §7(a) keeps the ban in place until Congress finds mining can be done without serious harm. §7(b) ends the Act after 10 years regardless, so the ban lapses without any such finding and §7(a) is largely meaningless.

24. **§7(a), mechanism.** There is no requirement, deadline, or funding for the National Academies report, and "serious harm" is undefined. The bill doesn't say whether the joint resolution itself ends the prohibition or what regime would follow. As a joint resolution it also requires presentment, so it is subject to a veto.

25. **§7(b), sunset effects.** There is no savings clause for pre-sunset violations, pending enforcement, or penalties, so it is unclear whether those can be pursued afterward. Because §8 delays the effective date, the ban actually runs only about 9.5 years.

26. **§8, 180-day gap.** Operators can ramp up, secure financing, and pursue licenses before the ban applies, and the registry won't capture activity in that period. The bill also sets no deadline for implementing rules before the effective date.

## Structural gaps

27. **No implementation provisions.** The bill designates no lead agency, grants no rulemaking authority, authorizes no appropriations, and says nothing on judicial review or standing. Each of these slows or weakens enforcement.

28. **No severability clause.** If a vulnerable provision (§2(1)(B), §5) is struck down, there is no express statement that the rest survives. Courts generally presume severability, but an explicit clause would remove the argument.

29. **Litigation exposure from line-drawing.** Treating existing license holders differently from applicants with pending applications or sunk investments could support takings, due process, or equal protection claims. The ban's application to activity on the high seas could also draw challenges under international-law freedoms.

Some of these problems cut in opposite directions: items 3 and 4 are overbreadth risks that make the bill easier to challenge, while items 1, 5, 8, and 9 are underbreadth gaps that let companies continue. For the markup preview, it may be worth presenting them separately. I'd also have counsel or CRS confirm the existing-law cross-references (item 13) before we publish anything on them.
